A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Learning in Structured Stackelberg Games. All 27 pages of v1 and 42 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support matching text, equations, algorithms, figures, and tables.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical guarantees, proofs, and constructed game examples, without original experiments, simulations, or data analyses.

after.justification: V2 remains theoretical throughout its main text and appendices. Its numerical examples and decision-list guarantees are analytically derived, without empirical evaluation.

M1.justification: V1's SSOA selects among individual followers' optimal strategies using remaining mistake dimension. V2's Algorithm 1 instead minimizes instantaneous worst-case regret plus remaining weighted dimension over the full simplex; the earlier procedure survives as MSSOA in Algorithm 4. V2 also introduces a minimax distributional learner and a decision-list learner. The retained S-ERM objective changes from strategy-mismatch minimization to empirical-utility maximization.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or instantiated experimental tasks for training or evaluation. The added decision-list class and game constructions are theoretical examples.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical baseline comparisons. SOA, ERM, and the retained mistake-based learner are compared through mathematical arguments.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an experimental evaluation protocol. The new cutoff-loss definitions and changed game assumptions concern theoretical learning guarantees, assessed under T1.

E4.justification: Neither version reports empirical ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness evaluations, or case studies. Added and revised counterexamples support theoretical proofs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. PAC failure probabilities and randomized lower-bound arguments are theoretical guarantees.

E6.justification: There are no measured experimental results in either version. Revised payoff constructions and derived regret values, including v2's 3/4 < 1 < 2 separation in Lemma B.6, are theoretical changes assessed under T1.

T1.justification: V2 replaces the main binary-tree-depth SL dimension with a supremum of minimax-weighted tree values and supplies instance-specific deterministic regret bounds; the old dimension remains as MSL in Appendix B. It adds gamma-SN and gamma-SG dimensions, cutoff sample complexity, distributional lower and upper bounds, an alternative edge-weighted characterization, and a decision-list learnability proof. Section 2 also changes follower tie-breaking from favoring the leader to a fixed known ordering. Retained proofs and payoff constructions receive substantive revisions.

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes mistake-based regret guarantees in realizable and agnostic settings and a single SN-dimensional ERM characterization. V2 centers its contributions on instance-optimal realizable regret and separate gamma-SN lower and gamma-SG upper sample-complexity bounds with an improper learner. Agnostic results remain in the appendix, but v2 explicitly excludes them from its instance-optimal characterization.

C2.justification: V2's Appendix B explains that strategy-misprediction bounds depend on leader tie-breaking and treat unequal utility losses equally. Sections 5–6 newly qualify applicability: the optimal online algorithm is computationally inefficient, efficient special cases may have suboptimal regret, and instance-optimal agnostic guarantees remain unresolved. These substantially clarify the meaning and limits of the results.

D1.justification: The linear-programming reduction and approximate-extreme-point details already appear in v1 and are retained. V2 adds mathematical algorithm specifications and complexity arguments, without separate implementation settings, hardware information, or code/data-access disclosures.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 substantially revises the positioning toward realizable regression, online learning beyond multiclass prediction, and piecewise-Lipschitz learning. New references include Attias et al., Daskalakis and Golowich, and several dispersion-related works. Much of the earlier Bayesian Stackelberg and application-domain discussion, with its associated references, is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, related work, and central exposition are extensively rewritten. Earlier main-text mistake-based online and distributional analyses are reorganized into Appendix B. V2 introduces a computational-complexity section and expands the conclusion into several explicit future directions.

P2.justification: V2 changes page format and increases body-text size throughout. It adds a results-summary table and explicit four-follower payoff tables, redraws the threshold schematic as Figure 3, and introduces follower-labelled SL trees in Figure 2. The earlier strategy-labelled trees remain as Appendix Figure 4. These changes extend substantially beyond renumbering and numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V2's minimax online learner addresses v1's coarse mistake-count proxy, while its computational and agnostic limitations are stated more clearly. However, the central new distributional guarantee has unresolved proof issues: Theorem 4.14 states a single-log sample bound, whereas its proof uses an n^{O(d log n)} counting bound that introduces an additional logarithmic factor. The proof also controls pairwise hypothesis losses without establishing the necessary connection to Algorithm 2's maximum over all consistent follower types. These gaps make the net quality improvement uncertain despite the substantial online advances.
